subject: Hex OS suites: 10 of 11 Chromium suites still fail anonymously on browser death
description:
Follow-on from 345. hex-shell-process.test.js now records page forensics (page labels, renderer-crash flag, browser.connected) and names a harness fault so deploy.sh stops calling it a shell regression. The other TEN suites that call puppeteer.launch have NO unhandled-rejection diagnosis at all: api-degradation-a11y, tenant-containment, terminal-async-output, safe-entry, first-timer, doc-examples, whatsnew-tenant, tenant-crosstab, md100-cmdlet-help, pwa. This matters BECAUSE of what 345 measured: the captured signature was browser.connected=FALSE (the Chromium PROCESS died) with crash=none and the page still open -- not a renderer crash, not a page teardown. A dying browser under concurrency would hit several suites AT ONCE, and only one of them would be able to say so; the rest would produce anonymous stacks and read as product regressions. DO NOT paste the block into ten files -- a fix repeated across ten files belongs in one. Extract _tools/hexos/harness-forensics.js exporting register(page,label) + arm(browserGetter), then require it from each suite. Note the exit contract constraint discovered in 345: exit 2 is NOT available, seven post-verify call sites read rc 2 as 'puppeteer unavailable, skip' with no divergence flag, so the shared module must exit 1 (node's own default for both unhandledRejection and uncaughtException) and communicate via the printed marker, not the code. Callers filter output: deploy.sh keeps tail -3, post-verify keeps grep -E 'FAIL|passed', so any summary line must be LAST and contain FAIL to survive.
[2026-09-06 04:45] SCOPE ADDITION from the 345 review, and it is the one case where all the new instrumentation goes DARK. Everything shipped in 345 handles a fault that THROWS or REJECTS. It does nothing for browser.close() HANGING and never settling -- measured twice: one OOM repro reached teardown at 107 SECONDS, and an earlier repro had to be killed by a 120s timeout (exit 124). In a hang there is no exception for the handler to catch, so: no forensics file, no FAIL marker, no exit code, and deploy.sh's new harness-fault-vs-regression branch never executes because the script never returns. A deploy gate that HANGS is worse than one that fails, because a failure is information and a hang is mistaken for slowness. This was item E of the original design, deliberately deferred out of the instrument-only phase, and the reviewer asked specifically that it not fall out of scope now that the throw-based case is closed and feels like 'the fix'. It is NOT solved. Requirement when built: bound the teardown with a timeout and FORCE-KILL via browser.process().kill('SIGKILL') rather than merely stopping the await -- abandoning the promise converts a loud, visible hang into a silent zombie Chromium accumulating on the deploy host, which is a worse steady state. Emit the same FAIL harness-fault marker on that path so the existing deploy.sh branch picks it up with no further shell change.
[2026-09-06 05:23] MODULE BUILT AND FIRST SUITE ADOPTED. b6e494c00 (_tools/hexos/harness-forensics.js + doc-examples adoption), ccf6d827f (the same read guard carried back to hex-shell-process). NINE SUITES REMAIN: safe-entry (Tier A, dual gate), pwa + tenant-crosstab + tenant-containment (Tier B, blocking pre-deploy gate 3.8), whatsnew-tenant + first-timer + api-degradation-a11y (Tier C, post-verify only), md100-cmdlet-help + terminal-async-output (Tier D, wired into NOTHING -- see 353; adopt these LAST, instrumenting a suite no gate reads buys almost nothing). ADOPTION ORDER IS DELIBERATE: cheapest and least dangerous first. Do NOT start with the Tier-B blocking gates; landing an unproven module first on the files you are most worried about maximises exposure to the risk. THE MODULE IS SMALLER THAN hex-shell-process's version ON PURPOSE: eight of the ten target suites drive at most ONE page and three go through browser.createBrowserContext() + ctx.newPage(), so labels/Map/targetcreated solve a problem they do not have. It keeps BOTH crash signals -- that was a review correction of mine. I proposed dropping the per-page listener for browser.connected alone, which is backwards: under a REPRODUCED renderer OOM page.on('error') fired while isClosed() stayed false and browser.connected stayed TRUE, whereas browser.connected=false came from a single self-inflicted kill. MANDATORY PER-SUITE STEP, now written into the module header rather than left as tribal knowledge: completed() has NO observable effect on a passing run, so clean runs prove NOTHING about whether it is placed correctly, and a mistake makes a confident FALSE claim about whether the suite was verified. Every adoption must inject a fault BEFORE and AFTER the completed() call and confirm both messages plus survival through tail -3 and grep -E 'FAIL|passed'. Placement genuinely differs per suite: hex-shell-process prints its tally BEFORE teardown, doc-examples tears down in finally and prints AFTER, so completed() goes at the end of the try. Copying a line position from another suite is not a substitute for the injection.
[2026-09-06 20:58] COMPLETE: 11 of 11. d75df607c closes it (tenant-containment, tenant-crosstab, safe-entry, pwa, md100-cmdlet-help, terminal-async-output), after b6e494c00 (module + doc-examples) and aa705ea99 (first-timer, api-degradation-a11y). hex-shell-process carries its own richer inline version from 345. EVERY SUITE NEEDED A DIFFERENT WIRING -- eleven suites, eleven shapes, and none could have been done by copying a line position from another file: tally BEFORE teardown (hex-shell-process, safe-entry) vs AFTER (doc-examples, first-timer, whatsnew-tenant, terminal-async, tenant-*, pwa); a browser RELAUNCHED mid-run so wiring had to go inside boot() (api-degradation-a11y); a page built inside a visit() helper (tenant-containment); one page per loop iteration (terminal-async-output); and a suite that closes its browser then keeps asserting (md100-cmdlet-help). A ten-file sweep would have got several wrong WHILE EVERY SUITE STILL PASSED, because completed() has no observable effect on a healthy run. VERIFICATION: all 11 pass the required both-direction injection (fault before completed() -> 'NOTHING WAS VERIFIED'; fault in teardown -> 'the suite WAS verified'), both routing to the harness-fault branch and surviving tail -3 and grep -E 'FAIL|passed'. Full sweep after wiring: 11/11 rc 0, 362 assertions, no fault logs on healthy runs. THE VERIFIER ITSELF HAD THREE DEFECTS, each of which would have produced a FALSE PASS, and they are worth knowing before anyone writes the next one: (1) anchoring on the literal 'F.browser(' also matches the COMMENT above the real call, so the probe injected into a comment while grep -c still reported success -- caught by the repo QC hook; (2) copies must pin EVERY __dirname-derived path, not just _app -- md100 resolves a lab HTML fixture too, so enumerating individual paths was the wrong approach and replacing __dirname wholesale was right; (3) a probe on a 2500ms timer RACES the suite -- safe-entry finishes 18 assertions faster than that, so the timer fired after completed() and the report said 'the suite WAS verified', which was TRUE and therefore a meaningless test of the before-case. It initially looked like safe-entry had a wiring bug; the measurement was the bug. Immediate rejection is deterministic. STILL OPEN, tracked here: browser.close() HANGING produces no exception, no exit code and no forensics -- the instrument goes dark and a hanging gate is worse than a failing one. Requires a bounded teardown with a real SIGKILL, not just abandoning the await.
